reason: This leg (VZ 20/MO 17/C 13/BTI 10/PFE 8, 32% cash) is only 11 trading days old (entered 2026-09-08) and every leg's fundamentals are intact: no dividend has been cut or put at real risk (VZ ex-div 10/9 at $0.707, BTI ex-div 10/2 at $0.835, MO forward yield 6.39%, PFE forward yield 6.22% all confirmed still being paid), no earnings disaster has landed (VZ and BTI don't report until late Oct/Nov, PFE not until 11/3, and C's Q2 print actually raised its 2026 RoTCE outlook above 11% with a Truist Buy reiterated), and P/Es remain in the cheap 10-15x band across the book (C 14.2x, MO 14.6x, BTI 14.3x trailing/10.7x forward, PFE mid-teens). The one real macro fact I found -- Fed funds holding at 4.00% with the 10-year around 5% and futures pricing higher-for-longer through December -- is a headwind for rate-sensitive high-yielders like VZ (down ~5% on the month, Morgan Stanley Equal-Weight) and explains this leg's modest -0.7% weighted drag since entry, but it is a known, structural feature of a deep-value dividend mandate, not new information: I already knew when I built this book that these names are duration-sensitive, and nothing in this week's research (Barclays trimming MO's target to $58 while UBS stays Buy, UBS cutting C's target to $142 while Truist stays Buy) rises above normal analyst noise. Selling into an -0.7% short-term wobble to fund a rebuild would lock in real transaction costs (2bps/side equities plus the SEC/TAF tape on sells, on top of 32% cash already earning 4% APY as ballast) for no identified catalyst -- there is no credible dividend-cut, credit-event, or valuation-re-rating story on any of the five names as of 2026-09-19. The disciplined move for a deep-value dividend book is to let a genuinely cheap, income-generating basket ride through ordinary rate-driven noise rather than churn on an 11-day sample, so I am holding the book exactly as filled, unchanged into the 2026-09-21 close.
